Ford’s S650 Mustang Becomes a Lot More Practical in Fantasy Land With New Wagon Body Style
8 photos
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik
The seventh-generation Ford Mustang blew three candles off its birthday cake earlier this year, and just for kicks, we will remind you that it is the only muscle car in production to feature a V8 engine.
Actually, it boasts not just one but quit a few V8 powertrains, and even more if we start bringing the Shelby versions into discussion. And that’s something that has given Dodge a headache, as its electric and six-pot bet on the modern-day Charger hasn’t exactly paid off. Therefore, the Stellantis-owned brand is now considering a V8-powered version of the Charger. Moreover, the next-gen Chevy Camaro is also expected to launch with V8 power, though instead of a regular coupe body style, it might be offered solely as a four-door sedan.
That may not sound like a wise choice at first, but let’s not forget that the modern Dodge Charger is also offered as a four-door sedan, and if the bowtie company indeed goes down this route, then it will eventually force Ford’s hand to launch a similar version of the Mustang. And to be honest, that’s not a huge eyebrow-raiser, because such a thing has been rumored several times over the years. However, could the Blue Oval go beyond the traditional sedan and launch a station wagon variant of its pony car?
The answer to this question is obviously “no.” Nothing suggests that the Dearborn company plans to turn the S650 (or its successor that should still be a few good years away, as there’s no reason to believe that the ‘Stang won’t survive for the next generation) into an estate. Such a thing would be a very practical family car, and a low-riding alternative to traditional crossovers and SUVs, and between us, it would not be bad at all. That’s my opinion, anyway, and before asking you to reveal yours, we will delve into it.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik And by “it,” we mean the five-door version of the S650 Ford Mustang that was rendered by @kelsonik and shared on social media recently. This thing retains the traditional design of the pony car at the front. Further back, it has a longer roofline that is arched toward the rear. It also features four instead of two doors, and the front ones are shorter. Out back, it sports the same design overall, albeit with a tailgate rather than a trunk lid, complete with a large spoiler attached to it, and a windscreen wiper.
The tailgate opens up into a very generous cargo area that could easily eat a few large suitcases, thus making this model the perfect car for a week-long getaway. The space between the axles has also been enlarged, thus translating to more legroom for the backseat occupants, though the headroom for those sitting at the rear does not seem to be very good. Another interesting novelty is the frameless design of the side windows, which makes this model look a lot sportier.
The car sits a bit closer to the ground than usual, has some skirts on the lower parts of the body all around, and rides on wheels that seem to be brand new. The alloys are concave, larger than the OEM ones, and feature a Y-spoke design. The sport a black finish in these CGIs, and they’re joined by other black elements on the outside. The rest of the car has a red look, and the interior is home to black leather upholstery, as far as we can see.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik It looks like the quoted rendering artist has imagined the Ford Mustang Wagon in the Dark Horse SC configuration. This is the range-topping version of the brand’s pony car, in case you forgot, and it is pretty much the modern-day equivalent of the S550-based Shelby GT500. It packs a 5.2-liter supercharged V8 engine, and has 795 horsepower (806 ps/593 kW) and 660 lb-ft (895 Nm) of torque available via the right pedal, delivered to the rear axle through a Tremec 7-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission.
That’s a healthy jump over the older Ford Mustang Shelby GT500, which had 760 hp (771 ps/567 kW) and 627 lb-ft (847 Nm) of torque on tap. This model hit 60 mph (97 kph) in a little over three seconds, and the modern-day Mustang Dark Horse SC is estimated to complete the sprint in less than three seconds, running the standing quarter mile in 10.8 seconds, as per third-party estimates.
Naturally, a station wagon version of this model would be a bit slower due to the extra weight, and would need proper chassis calibration if it wants to win more hearts. But as mentioned above, we would not hold our breath for such a thing, as it won’t happen. A Ford Mustang Sedan, on the other hand, seems quite possible. If you had to choose between a four-door and a five-door version of the S650 Mustang, which one would you get and why? View this post on Instagram A post shared by CAR DESIGN | RENDERINGS (@kelsonik)

source_document.body:

Mechanic Inspects a 250,000-Mile Toyota Pickup Truck and This Is What He Finds
17 photos
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube
The owner took his 1993 Toyota Pickup at a service shop for a milestone checkup. The vehicle has recently hit 250,000 miles at the respectable age of 33 years old. The mechanic has already informed the customer that he won't let it drive out of his shop before he checks everything about it. However, the owner refused to fix all the issues that he found.
Toyota Pickup is not just a simple way of referring to this model. That is exactly how Toyota officially named it in the United States and Canada, while it was sold as the Toyota Hilux in most other international markets. Toyota also introduced a larger, full-size truck model in 1993, called the T100.
Typical of Toyota, the fifth-generation compact trucks built by the Japanese firm between 1989 and 1995 are widely known for bombproof reliability, blocky early 1990s design, and mechanical simplicity. And yes, everything is mechanical and manual on the truck that just drove into the shop belonging to David Long, a.k.a. The Car Wizard.
It has power, nothing. It even comes with crank windows, just like Slate’s new electric truck, and it doesn't even have a single airbag on board. This truck rolled off the production line before such safety features became mandatory. Frontal airbags became mandatory for all new passenger cars and light trucks in the United States starting with the 1999 model year.
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube Back in the day, Toyota offered two engine options, so customers could go home with either the 2.4-liter inline-four, which produced 116 horsepower and 140 pound-feet of torque, or the 3.0-liter V6 engine, as this truck has.
The V6 pushes out 150 horsepower (152 metric horsepower) and 180 pound-feet (244 Newton meters) of torque. A five-speed manual transmission puts the power down through all four corners. The truck can tow up to 3,500 pounds (1,588 kilograms). But as bulletproof as the Toyota Pickup may have been in its era, time is catching up with it. It did age like fine wine, but it aged. It's only natural.
The last time the Toyota pickup truck went through proper, thorough maintenance work was back in 1997 when it had 103,000 miles (165,762 kilometers) on the clock. That is nearly 30 years and 150,000 miles (241,402 kilometers) ago.
The mechanic is now desperately trying to make up for the lost time. That is if the owner will let him. But sourcing parts for a truck that old has been a massive challenge, because he couldn’t find a single shop out there that has all the parts.
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube Besides, the Wizard has a long list of issues that he has to deal with. The air conditioning is not working, and the owner doesn’t even consider fixing it or finding out why it doesn’t work, because he doesn’t want to pay for the procedure. So this is as far as the mechanical investigation goes.
The all-wheel-drive system doesn't work either, and the conversation between the mechanic and the owner stopped with " I don't want it fixed ." Furthermore, the power steering fluid has turned brown, the timing cover has oil leaking all over, and the timing belt is nearly 30 years old. When he gets that apart, he will figure out the source of the leak.
The Wizard already installed a new distributor, ignition, spark plugs, and wires. The fuel filter also needs to be changed because it has been eaten by rust. The rear differential is leaking, and the transmission and transfer case are due for a fluid change as well.
The truck no longer has a windshield washer system. It didn’t simply vanish over the years. The owner admitted that he was in the midst of doing some repairs, probably in his own garage or driveway, and will put it back in when he's done.
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube While many trucks wearing different badges are not even on the road anymore, having been either scrapped or left to rot in junkyards, this one hasn’t suffered any catastrophic failure over all these years. It still has the original engine and transmission.
At exactly 252,919 miles (407,030 kilometers) and after 33 years on the road, even the bulletproof Toyota Truck is battling corrosion, despite spending its entire life in New Mexico. The corrosion might be the result of some rough off-roading and riverbed crossing.
A pinion seal is leaking even though the owner has recently gotten it replaced. The Wizard told him to take it back to where he got it repaired and have it fixed again for no extra cost, because it should be covered by warranty.
Another major issue the truck came with is the old tires, which show dangerous cracks. They are date-coded 2001. That explains it! They need to be replaced ASAP, especially because the owner is planning to go on a road trip with his Toyota Truck, even though he has only approved the tune-up and the timing belt fixes.
The owner is well aware that the cost of repairs might be more than the actual cost of the truck. The mechanic told him he could sell it for as much as $10,000, while the repairs would cost less than half of that.
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube The Car Wizard says the investment is definitely worth it because once it gets fully repaired, the good, old Toyota Truck can easily hit 750,000 miles (1,207,008 kilometers). " This is one of the best trucks that you could buy on planet Earth, " he says.

source_document.body:
North American cross-border trucking capacity is expected to remain constrained into 2027 despite softer freight demand.
Executives at logistics provider TRAFFIX told FreightWaves driver shortages , regulatory restrictions and rising operating costs could limit the number of trucks available to haul goods between the U.S., Mexico and Canada.
The challenges are being compounded by higher interest rates and tighter lending conditions that are discouraging new trucking companies from entering the market, preventing the kind of capacity expansion that followed the freight rate surge during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“We’re only four or five years later and we’re not seeing that,” Alex Fuller, vice president of commercial intelligence at TRAFFIX, told FreightWaves in an interview. “And it’s like, OK, well, what’s different?”
Fuller said two factors stand out: tighter regulations governing who can operate commercial trucks and the increased cost of purchasing equipment.
During the pandemic, prospective owner-operators could finance trucks with relatively inexpensive loans and government stimulus funds. Today, Fuller said, financing costs can reach 8% to 9%, making it much more difficult for drivers to enter the industry or established carriers to expand their fleets.
“Because of that, yeah, rates are going to stay higher for longer ,” Fuller said. “And we’re not going to see the immediate drop like we saw a couple of years ago in rates.”
The comments follow the release of TRAFFIX’s October North American Cross-Border Index , which measures freight market pressures along the U.S.-Mexico and U.S.-Canada corridors.
The index registered 57 for Canada and 54 for Mexico, down one point each from September. Readings above 50 indicate tighter market conditions, including elevated costs, limited truck capacity and regulatory challenges.
Although shipment volumes remain relatively soft, TRAFFIX said available truck capacity has shown little improvement, leaving shippers with fewer alternatives when contracted carriers are unable to cover loads.
The index tracks four components — transportation costs, capacity, demand and trade policy — using more than 10 economic, freight and trade indicators.
Fuller said the index relies primarily on publicly available government and trade data, which TRAFFIX compares with its internal freight activity to assess whether the findings reflect conditions experienced by its customers and carriers.
As of Oct. 11, FreightWaves SONAR’s Outbound Tender Volume Index (STVI.LRD) for Laredo has climbed sharply from 39.95 in mid-September to 51.95, indicating a solid uptick in cross-border freight demand. This demand push is reflected in the SONAR Weighted Rejection Index (SWRI), which flipped from -0.74 last week to +0.65, confirming that capacity in Laredo and its adjacent areas is actively tightening.
The Laredo market’s outbound volumes surged in October (STVI.LRD up to 51.95), outpacing last week’s levels and driving capacity constraints.To learn more about FreightWaves SONAR, click here .
Mexico faces driver shortages, visa restrictions
Patricio Gutierrez, TRAFFIX’s Manzanillo, Mexico-based carrier sales manager, said the country’s cross-border trucking industry is confronting a combination of driver shortages, U.S. immigration restrictions and structural bottlenecks at border crossings.
“I think that the main issue here is a lack of qualified drivers,” Gutierrez said, pointing to Mexican drivers holding valid B-1 visas and the limited number of trucks authorized to operate in the United States.
He said cross-border operations require drivers and equipment that meet specific regulatory requirements, reducing the number of carriers able to handle international shipments.
Border delays and longer transit times further restrict usable capacity by keeping trucks occupied longer, even when overall shipment demand remains relatively stable.
Gutierrez also highlighted Mexico’s longstanding difficulties recruiting younger truck drivers.
He said many drivers are in their 50s and 60s, while younger workers are reluctant to enter the profession because of security concerns and relatively low compensation.
“The shortage of drivers in Mexico is a real problem,” Gutierrez said.
The capacity constraints are especially important at major commercial gateways such as Laredo, Texas, where large concentrations of cross-border freight make certain routes particularly sensitive to equipment and driver availability.
A separate October freight market report from C.H. Robinson supports concerns about Mexico’s shrinking pool of qualified cross-border drivers.
The company’s Edge Report said U.S. authorities have withdrawn visas from approximately 25,000 Mexican freight drivers, citing Mexican trucking association CANACAR.
C.H. Robinson said continued B-1 visa withdrawals and temporary border disruptions reduced usable truck capacity during September, even as load-to-truck ratios and freight volumes remained relatively stable at major Texas crossings.
The report also highlighted restrictions on southbound empty-truck crossings at Eagle Pass and Brownsville, Texas, from Sept. 9-14.
During the disruptions, daily commercial crossings reportedly fell from approximately 1,000 to between 300 and 400, while nearly 700 tractors were stranded on the U.S. side of the border.
Some carriers were forced to reposition equipment through Laredo, adding mileage, fuel costs and transit time.
C.H. Robinson warned that qualified driver availability could tighten further as fourth-quarter shipping volumes increase.
Canada carriers struggle with imbalanced freight flows
On the U.S.-Canada border, TRAFFIX executives said trade tensions and changing freight patterns are creating a different set of challenges.
Lance Halliday, TRAFFIX’s Toronto-based regional director of carrier sales, said trucking companies are struggling with an imbalance between freight moving from Canada into the United States and shipments returning north.
He said demand for Canadian exports remains relatively strong, but weaker south-to-north freight flows make it difficult for drivers to find return loads.
“There’s still a severe lack of inbound,” Halliday said. “So there’s not a lot of freight coming in from the U.S. into Canada right now.”
That imbalance has made some carriers unwilling to accept shipments into certain U.S. markets without significantly higher compensation.
Halliday singled out Florida as an especially challenging destination because drivers may have to wait days for a return shipment or travel hundreds of miles empty to find another load.
“Florida is a no-go zone,” Halliday said. “Guys just won’t go because they’re getting stuck down there for days.”
He said carriers are also increasingly reluctant to accept freight into markets where the cost of returning empty equipment could eliminate profits.
The imbalance is contributing to rising transportation rates, particularly on lanes where shippers have limited carrier alternatives.
Halliday said rates on some corridors have climbed 25% to 35% over roughly the past month to month and a half, although he did not identify specific lanes or provide a marketwide average.
Contract freight shifts toward spot market
TRAFFIX executives also described a growing shift toward transactional freight as carriers reject previously negotiated contract rates.
Halliday said some carriers are returning freight commitments because rates established months earlier no longer cover their operating costs.
That has forced shipments farther down shippers’ carrier-selection lists, increasing reliance on spot-market transportation.
“We’re seeing a lot of that contractual freight handed back by their primary carriers,” Halliday said.
He said the volume of transactional freight opportunities TRAFFIX is seeing on the Canadian side has surpassed levels experienced during the COVID-19 freight market, based on his observations of the company’s operations.
Gutierrez said similar conditions are emerging in Mexico, where rising diesel costs and capacity restrictions are pushing carriers to seek higher rates.
He said some Mexican shippers remain reluctant to accept higher transportation costs, creating tension between carriers trying to maintain profitability and customers accustomed to lower contract pricing.
Both executives said the situation reflects broader structural challenges rather than a temporary increase in diesel prices.
Halliday pointed to higher driver wages, insurance expenses and reduced access to financing as additional pressures preventing carriers from expanding.
Capacity constraints could extend into 2027
Looking ahead, TRAFFIX executives said they expect cross-border truck capacity to remain tight through the end of 2026 and into next year.
Halliday said he does not expect significant relief over the next three to six months, citing continuing driver shortages, trade uncertainty and seasonal capacity reductions.
“I think that in the short term, it’s going to continue to tighten up,” Halliday said. “I don’t think that there’s any way that this changes over the next three to six months.”
Gutierrez said Mexico faces similar longer-term challenges unless the industry finds ways to recruit drivers and improve cross-border operating efficiency.
Fuller said the lack of new capacity entering the market could keep freight rates elevated even without a substantial recovery in demand.
Unlike the pandemic-era trucking boom, when high rates encouraged new carriers to purchase equipment and enter the industry, today’s financing environment is discouraging that response.
Why it matters: Shippers face the prospect of elevated freight rates and fewer carrier options even as shipment demand remains relatively soft, TRAFFIX executives say.

Ford took its all-new Ranger MS-RT Champion Edition to Paris to brag about the motorsport-inspired street truck, built based on a collaboration between Ford Pro and the tuning firm MS-RT. The model features a bold styling package, while fully maintaining the workhorse credentials.
The Ford Ranger MS-RT Champion Edition builds on all the qualities that made the Ranger Europe’s best-selling pickup truck. The Champion Edition is finished exclusively in Agate Black paint with striking gold racing stripes running across the hood, doors, and sides.
The truck features aggressive wide-body flared fenders, widening the track by 1.6 inches (40 millimeters) on each side, a unique honeycomb grille and an integrated front bumper splitter up front, and a distinctive ducktail tailgate spoiler, along with a faux rear diffuser out back.
The Ranger MS-RT Champion Edition rides on massive 21-inch gold diamond-cut alloy wheels and sits on a suspension setup that lowers it by 1.6 inches (40 millimeters) compared to a stock Ranger. It features firmer front dampers and a custom-tuned rear suspension geometry, engineered for responsive street handling and more precise steering.
Photo: Ford The lowered suspension and aerodynamic styling make it more aggressive, but do not compromise the Ranger's heavy-duty truck capability. It still retains its one-ton payload capacity and can tow up to 7,716 pounds (3,500 kilograms).
The street race personality of the Ranger MS-RT is also visible inside the four-door double cab, which hosts sports seats in premium eco-leather and suede with highly supportive bolstering, contrasting gold stitching, and the MS-RT badges embroidered on the seatbacks.
A heated steering wheel with gold stitching and a 12 o’clock mark, custom gold floor mats, and an exclusive "Champion Edition" numbered plaque on the center console are also on the menu. The cabin also hosts the portrait-oriented 12-inch SYNC 4 touchscreen, alongside dual-zone climate control and 360-degree Zone Lighting.
Buyers can choose between the two engine options available. The 3.0-liter EcoBlue V6 turbodiesel generates 237 horsepower (240 metric horsepower) and 443 pound-feet (600 Newton meters of torque) for an acceleration from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph) in 8.7 seconds and a top speed of 112 mph (180 kph). A ten-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners with the help of a full-time four-wheel drive.
Photo: Ford The other powertrain option offered by Ford with the special edition is the 2.3-liter EcoBoost Plug-in Hybrid, which pairs the 2.3-liter four-cylinder gas engine with an electric motor. Together they produce 277 horsepower (281 metric horsepower) and 514 pound-feet (697 Newton meters) of torque.
Those make the Ranger accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 9.0 seconds on its way to the same top speed of 112 mph. An 11.8-kWh battery pack stores enough energy to make the truck travel up to 26 miles (roughly 40 kilometers) on electric power only.
Production is capped at only 500 units in Europe, with each dual-cab vehicle being hand-finished by MS-RT (M-Sport Road Technology) in the United Kingdom. Order books are officially open through European Ford Pro commercial networks, and deliveries are slated to begin next spring.
Because this vehicle has been developed exclusively as a European specialty series, there are no active plans to launch it in the United States market. Ford hasn’t disclosed any pricing details, so we probably have to wait until next year to find out more.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed the detailed expenses for which Poland will allocate the loan received under the SAFE program. (Photo: Chancellery of the Prime Minister)
WARSAW — The prime minister of Poland today used his keynote address at a security conference here to attempt to rally Europe to do more to combat what he said was the “real threat” from Russia.
“No one wants escalation or war. We all dream of peace,” Donald Tusk said to an audience of European political, military and defense industry figures. “The path to peace does not lie through weakness. The path to peace lies in stopping the aggressor with all available means and forces.”
Tusk said Russia would “not stop” with Ukraine and, given the chance, would seek to “reshape Poland’s security architecture” in a bid to “dismantle the security architecture in Europe so that Russian dominance returns to the state it was before 1989. We have no doubt about this.”
Tusk said a new NATO “theory of victory,” revealed in a separate speech today by Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Alexus Grynkewich left him “filled with optimism.”
In Grynkewich, he said, he “had a partner who also harbors no illusions, no miconceptions, regarding Russia’s intentions toward Ukraine, as well as toward Europe and the entire world.”
The prime minister said he was traveling to Brussels to call on Europe to increase pressure on Europe and toughen sanctions targeting Moscow.
“Ukraine will not be broken or intimidated. Poland will not be broken or intimidated. Europe, NATO, and the entire free world will not be broken or intimidated. That message must go out today from every capital—from Warsaw to Washington,” concluded Tusk.
Immediately following Tusk’s address, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued his own virtual address to the audience, saying that Moscow had launched attacks on Ukrainian cities despite US President Donald Trump’s claim that both sides had agreed not to strike energy targets.
“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people,” he said.
Zelenskyy also claimed that recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers had diminished the amount of disinformation online — suggesting the centers had been used by Russian online provocateurs.
A day after Trump announced a controversial oil deal with Russia, Zelenskyy implored the US to not give “concessions” but instead put “real pressure” on Moscow.
To Poland, Zelenskyy said Warsaw and Kyiv were “natural allies.”
“And when we stand together, Russia has no chance,” he said. “We need to end Russia’s war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together, Europe and the United States.”

Blink-182 and You Missed It: Travis Barker Has Jay Leno Screaming in His 500-HP 1959 Impala Ragtop
53 photos
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage
Travis Barker is the rhythmic powerhouse behind Blink-182, but his journey extends far beyond the confines of music. Born to a steel mill worker in Fontana, he developed a profound appreciation for classic automobiles while watching his father wrench on broken-down Cadillacs in their backyard. The kid was hooked for life, and his 1959 Chevrolet Impala custom is solid proof that some addictions need no cure.
Reflecting on those formative years, he shared a personal memory, noting, "My dad would come home every day, I would be playing drums in my garage, he would open the garage, bring his Harley in, and I'm still ten times louder than his Harley" This foundational experience shaped his very deep automotive passion, proving that his mechanical inclination rivals his immense musical talent.
Beyond his artistic achievements, his life story is one of profound resilience and personal triumph, a narrative heavily shaped by a horrific 2008 plane crash. Surviving that tragic event left him with severe physical and emotional scars, altering his perspective on life and encouraging him to rebuild himself from the ground up.
Emerging stronger than before, he eventually conquered his paralyzing fear of flying. "In 2017 when we started it there was no ending to it 'cause I was still not flying... it was like a nice light at the end of the tunnel, being able to tell my story."
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage His recent appearance on Jay Leno's Garage provided fans with a rare glimpse into his personal sanctuary, where vintage American steel takes center stage, sidelining the hi-hats and toms for which he is famed the world over. The drummer showcased his prized 1959 Chevrolet Impala convertible, a stunning machine that is the perfect capsule of the vibrant and bright SoCal car culture.
Admiring the iconic vehicle, Jay Leno remarked, "I remember when it came out, Chevy had this whole thing like “these aerodynamic wings, these help stabilize the car at high speed,” all this phony stuff, it was just a styling exercise." This vehicle perfectly bridges his childhood memories of massive cruisers with a contemporary taste for high-end automotive craftsmanship. This is no ordinary ’59.
The 1959 Chevrolet Impala represents a watershed moment in American automotive history, marking the very first year it became a standalone model line. Shedding its previous Bel Air legacy status, the massive cruiser introduced wildly flamboyant styling cues, including those iconic horizontal teardrop taillights – the unmistakable “cat eyes,“ and massive flat rear fins.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage Its dramatic aesthetic perfectly mirrored the futuristic optimism of the late 1950s, turning the humble Chevy into a cultural beacon for an entire generation. General Motors pushed the boundaries of automotive design during this era, overhauling their entire lineup on an almost annual basis to keep consumers captivated.
The 1959 styling was a radical departure from the 1958 models, representing a complete reimagining of the full-size Chevrolet platform that stunned the buying public. This single-year design remains highly coveted among collectors precisely because it boldly captures unrestrained mid-century American automotive design exuberance and passion.
During that pivotal season, Chevrolet manufactured 1,528,592 vehicles, though the company only recorded production numbers categorized by body style rather than specific models, engines, or transmissions.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage The factory produced 525,461 four-door sedans, 281,924 two-door sedans, 182,520 sport sedans, 164,901 sport coupes, 188,623 four-door station wagons, and 20,760 two-door station wagons. Meanwhile, the stunning convertible variant saw 72,765 units roll off the assembly line, making it quite rare in comparison to the whole volume.
The original factory base price for a 1959 convertible equipped with the entry-level six-cylinder engine was set at 2,849 dollars. Upgrading to the standard V8 engine pushed that starting figure to 2,967 dollars, before buyers even began ticking boxes for power steering or highly desirable convenience accessories.
The striking black-on-black convertible showcased by Travis Barker on Jay Leno's Garage is a masterful blend of immaculate preservation and tasteful modernization. Purchased from a Texas owner, the flawless exterior still presents a mirror-like finish.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage Originally, this massive land yacht came with the venerable 348 cubic-inch big-block engine and a massive factory steering wheel that constantly brushed against the driver. To transform this beautiful boulevard cruiser into a reliable daily driver, the rocker initiated a full overhaul while meticulously preserving the vintage aesthetic.
The vintage 348 powerplant was replaced by a modern LS3 crate engine, delivering an adrenaline-overdosing 495 horsepower. Describing the duality of the driving experience, he noted, "It's like two personalities: one cruiser, one bruiser."
This substantial increase in reliable power ensures the heavy convertible navigates modern traffic with ease, while retaining its timeless, classic low-rider swagger. Bringing the 495 horsepower to a halt requires serious stopping capabilities, so the factory drum setup was upgraded to modern engineering standards.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage Wilwood disc brakes now occupy the corners, offering the precise stopping performance demanded by the spirited LS3 powerhouse. Additionally, a custom Magnaflow exhaust system was integrated, emitting a deep, throaty rumble that complements the aggressive nature of the LS3 engine.
The interior received enhancements to maximize driving comfort without ruining the nostalgic cabin atmosphere that defines vintage full-size General Motors craftsmanship. A pristine red interior provides a striking visual contrast against the jet-black exterior, looking entirely period-correct despite subtle aftermarket refinements.
The bulky steering wheel was swapped for a smaller, more maneuverable replacement, allowing the driver ample legroom to operate the massive vehicle without restrictions. Cruising through the sweltering California heat demands functional climate control, a necessity addressed by a Vintage Air conditioning unit.
Photo: YouTube/Jay Leno's Garage Utilizing clever adapters, the modern cooling system operates through the factory dashboard sliders, maintaining the unblemished original appearance of the instrument cluster. Visually, the vehicle achieves its distinct low-rider cool through an adjustable air ride suspension system that dictates the ground clearance.
While driving heavily slammed is impractical for standard road conditions, the lift kit allows the owner to navigate uneven blacktops before dropping to an almost pancake stance at automotive events. Brilliant 14-inch Dayton wire wheels wrap up the exterior aesthetics, complementing the Continental kit extending off the rear.
This 1959 Impala ragtop custom is an effortless Sunday boulevard cruiser, yet instantly morphs into a fierce bruiser the moment the accelerator pedal goes intimate with the kick panel. It’s a great drum solo, if you will, one that ends a grand concert in style, leaving fans gasping for air in an afterburn of adrenaline and applause.

The company that previously operated as Elbit Systems’ American subsidiary made its AUSA expo debut this week as Twenty-Six Defense.
Under the new brand, the Texas-based defense firm debuted Primex , a lightweight wearable meant to provide soldiers with night-vision capabilities and augmented reality so they can “maintain awareness without distraction or cognitive overload.”
For the design, Twenty-Six Defense said it engineered Primex for sustained operational use by equipping it with “the lightest head-borne load and near-neutral center of gravity.”
The company explained Primex uses low-light sensors, thermal imagery, and real-time processing to produce an ultra-low-latency digital perception that enables operators to better interpret the surrounding area even amid challenging environmental conditions.
What separates Primex from other advanced lightweight heads-up display units for operators, according to Twenty-Six Defense, is that its design was built on mature technologies that have already been fielded.
The company said it already produces AN/PSQ-44 Enhanced Night Vision Goggles , which contain features that allow for rapid target acquisition and augment reality to enhance visual clarity.
In August, Ernie Basic, Twenty-Six Defense’s senior director of research and development, explained how his company was developing equipment for the Soldier Borne Mission Command , a project to deliver augmented reality wearables to soldiers.
He said the technology combines fighter-pilot displays with night-vision systems, so soldiers get “the full operational picture.”
“You are not only seeing what is in front of you. You can leverage a feed coming from a drone or from other assets,” he said. “You can start seeing what is going on behind a house or another structure, cue a squad to a different location, and continuously update them.”
In addition to Primex, Twenty-Six Defense showcased defensive weapons and equipment like the XM1168 mobile 120mm mortar system, Autonomous Relocatable Surveillance Tower and SkyStriker Block 4E.
About Daniel Terrill
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

Once America’s most popular electric pickup, Ford’s F-150 Lightning is finding a second life on the used market.
Ford F-150 Lightning finds buyers in the used market
The F-150 Lightning is hard to pass up at 50% to 60% off sticker price, even used. With new models no longer available , Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes on the used market.
After the last model rolled off the assembly line last December, CEO Jim Farley said the decision to end production came as the “very high-end EVs, the $50K, 70K, $80,000 vehicles, they just weren’t selling.”
At 50% to 60% off, it now looks like a bargain in the used market. “When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” Jimmy Douglas, CEO of Plug, a wholesale EV dealer, told Bloomberg .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
On the used market, however, “the Lightning is 50% to 60% of the sticker price and that is really a sweet spot,” he added.
Used Ford F-150 Lightnings are selling in about 20 days, less than half the 44-day average for used vehicles in the US. According to Edmunds.com , prices are now up 4% to about $50,000 since the start of the year.
2025 Ford F-150 Lightning (Source: Ford)
Douglass said that close to one-third of used models are sold by rival dealerships that would normally flip them back to Ford. However, many are opting to sell them directly because of demand.
Chase Norris from Colorado called the electric pickup a bargain. He purchased a used Lightning for around $40,000 and considers it a major upgrade from his previous gas F-150.
EV Group CEO and cofounder Alex Lawrence, which sells pre-owned electric vehicles, said he can’t get his hands on any reasonably priced used F-150 Lightnings currently.
Ford F-150 Lightning, Mustang Mach-E at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Ford)
He said many Lightning buyers use it as a second truck to save money during their weekly commute.
It looks essentially the same as the gas-powered F-150, offers instant torque, and produces zero tailpipe emissions, but the electric pickup failed to meet Ford’s expectations because of its higher price.
The base F-150 Lightning Pro debuted in 2021 with a starting MSRP of $39,974, but that was quickly raised to around $60,000 a year or so later.
2024 Ford F-150 Lightning Flash (Source: Ford)
According to Edmunds.com , the average transaction price for the F-150 Lightning in its first year of sales was $79,000 because Ford focused on higher-priced trims. The gas version’s ATP was about $19,000 less.
Even with the higher sticker price, Ford was losing a considerable amount on each Lightning it produced. In Q1 2024, Ford lost more than $100,000 on every EV it built.
Next year, Ford will take another crack at the electric pickup market with the Fathom, the first vehicle based on its “groundbreaking” new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Ford said the Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard-range version. Even with the $1,595 delivery fee included, the electric pickup will start at under $30,000.
As the first vehicle built on its UEV platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step-change from its first-generation EVs in efficiency and, for its sake, profitability.
According to Ford, the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4 and will be the first vehicle with Apple Maps directly integrated into the navigation system.
Ford’s midsize UEV pickup spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Reddit)
We also know the electric pickup will have a NACS port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger this summer.
Ford reportedly aims to sell around 100,000 Fathoms in its first year. CEO Jim Farley admitted at the 2026 Automotive News Congress that “It’s going to be a heck of an effort to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”
Meanwhile, a company spokesperson confirmed with Electrek that “We’ve said previously, ‘Fathom will launch in 2027 ‘- and there is no change to that.
Electrek’s Take
F-150 Lightning sales surging on the used market proves that buyers are looking for electric pickups at the right price.
At $60,000 to $70,000, the Lightning wasn’t so attractive, but at $40,000 used, it suddenly is. Perhaps Ford is on to something with its next-gen EV pickup, the Fathom, set to go on sale starting at under $30,000.
Will it deliver on its promise? Ford has yet to reveal battery specs, towing capacity, range, or any other specs. We should learn more soon.

source_document.body:
It’s about the size of the Kia PV5 and VW ID. Buzz. As “a real alternative to SUVs and saloons,” Renault’s E-Space Concept makes you want to love minivans again.
Renault reveals the E-Space Concept, an electric MPV
While minivans aren’t the first thing that comes to mind when you think of a “cool” or fun-to-drive vehicle, Renault is out to change that.
Renault unveiled the E-Space Concept at the Paris Motor Show on Monday, a modern-day take on its iconic minivan from the 80s.
Although it’s still a concept, the MPV is designed as an electric successor to the original Renault Espace from 1984.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
With an MPV-body style and open layout, Renault said the minivan offers “a real alternative to SUVs and saloons” that dominate the market.
The E-Space Concept measures 4,700 mm long, 2,020 mm wide, and 1,670 mm tall, or about the size of the Kia PV5 Passenger and VW ID. Buzz short-wheelbase (SWB). While it retains a similar design to the first Espace, the electric version features a modern twist.
Renault E-Space Concept (Source: Renault)
Designed to maximize efficiency, the concept sits lower than a traditional SUV, with smooth lines and a roof spoiler reminiscent of the Espace 2 and 3.
Inside, the designers created a fully glazed cabin inspired by Bauhaus architecture, and in particular, German-American architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.
As such, the glass roof and windows extend well beyond the already low waistline. With the low waistline, “you can see into the cabin when standing next to the car. And once again, you can drive with your elbows on the door,” said Romain Gauvin, Renault Brand Head of Advanced Design & Concept Cars.
Renault E-Space Concept (Source: Renault)
The double-hinged rear doors open to a spacious interior with six individual seats and a flat-floor design.
Inspired by the original 1984 Espace, the seats break free from the traditional bucket design with “lacquered shells ” that appear to be floating.
Renault E-Space Concept interior (Source: Renault)
Each seat can rotate. The second-row seats can swivel 180 degrees to create a “TGV train square” with the third row. Passengers in the second row have a standard folding tray table and a 12.3″ screen mounted on the headrests.
In the four-seat configuration, where the second-row seats fold, you can create a large table with a remote-control console.
Renault E-Space Concept interior (Source: Renault)
The console includes an air purifier, a small fridge, video game controllers, and last but not least, a game of Connect 4.
Ambient lighting runs across the cabin, while night lights are built into the speakers. Reading lights are also mounted on the rail in the center of the glass roof.
The concept features a massive pillar-to-pillar curved display, OpenR Panorama, plus a center infotainment screen. Both can swivel around a base behind the steering wheel.
Speaking of which, the compact steering wheel design features steer-by-wire technology that’s “free from all the physical constraints typically associated with steering,” according to Stéphane Maiore, Renault Brand Head of Interior Design.
Renault didn’t confirm whether or when we will see a production version of the E-Space , but hinted that it’s a “contemporary retake on travel and family mobility in the electric age” and “outlines its vision for the car of the future.”

source_document.body:
A GPU cluster can be healthy and a job running while the model makes little useful progress. Seeing why requires observability built around the training run, not isolated infrastructure components.
A large-scale training job can look healthy to nearly every conventional monitoring tool while quietly wasting much of its GPU allocation.
The nodes are up. Slurm reports that the job is running. Kubernetes shows healthy containers. GPU utilization is high. Network traffic is flowing. No CUDA out-of-memory errors have appeared, and the loss keeps getting logged.
Nevertheless, step times may have doubled. One rank may be holding back hundreds of others. GPUs may be occupied by communication kernels without moving the training run forward. The input pipeline may be starving the accelerators.
Each tool accurately describes the part of the system it was designed to observe. But distributed training does not live inside any one of those parts.
It crosses all of them.
HPCwire has examined the operational complexity AI brings to HPC sites and the gap between acquiring GPU capacity and turning it into productivity . Observability is one of the missing layers between the two.
( Frame-Stock-Footage/Shutterstock)
Filling that gap takes more than adding infrastructure metrics to a dashboard; observability itself must be rethought for how large-scale training behaves.
Four Views of the Same Training Run
Traditional observability grew around stable abstractions such as hosts, services, containers and requests, which work well when components can be examined separately.
Distributed training is different. A job temporarily assembles thousands of accelerators, processes, network links and storage paths into one synchronized system, where a slowdown anywhere can set the pace of the whole job.
Infrastructure monitoring, through tools such as NVIDIA’s Data Center GPU Manager , sees GPU activity, memory, power, temperature, clocks, hardware errors and interconnect traffic at low overhead.
Schedulers and orchestrators see allocations, queues, job states, container health, resource requests and placement decisions.
Runtime tools sit closer to the application: CUPTI exposes CUDA API calls, kernel activity and memory operations, and NCCL logs and profiler interfaces show communicator setup, collectives, topology and transport choices.
ML experiment tracking sees steps, epochs, throughput, loss, learning rate, checkpoints and model outputs.
Each view is valuable, but they are split by identifiers, time models, retention policies and owners. Infrastructure teams think in nodes and GPUs, platform teams in Slurm jobs or Kubernetes pods, ML engineers in experiments, runs and checkpoints.
When Accurate Metrics Become Misleading
Consider a distributed data-parallel job in which one training process begins receiving data more slowly than its peers.
It reaches gradient synchronization late, and the other ranks wait for it inside the collective. Their GPUs look active because NCCL kernels are resident, so cluster-wide utilization may still look respectable.
(Digineer Station/Shutterstock)
The infrastructure dashboard therefore shows busy GPUs. The communication dashboard shows long collectives. The training log shows slower steps. The storage dashboard may show elevated latency.
Viewed separately, they suggest competing culprits: a network bottleneck, inefficient collectives, overloaded storage or poorly tuned kernels.
On one timeline, compared by rank, the sequence is clear: one process hit an input delay, arrived late and made its peers wait.
The distinction matters because the long collective is not necessarily the original problem. It is where the problem became visible across the cluster.
The reverse also happens. During a planned checkpoint, quiet GPUs and heavy storage activity are correct, but a phase-blind alert will flag them as an incident.
Averages hide problems too. If a different rank straggles each step, every device’s average utilization can look the same; the imbalance shows only at rank and step granularity.
Then there are problems that infrastructure monitoring cannot recognize at all. A job can run without crashes, maintain high GPU activity and exit with code zero while the loss remains flat, diverges or becomes numerically invalid. Operationally, the workload succeeded. Scientifically, it failed.
Health is contextual: a metric means something only relative to the other ranks, the training phase and the model’s progress.
The Training Run Must Become the Primary Entity
Observability must treat the training run as a first-class entity, tying together at minimum:
Nvidia NVL72
Experiment and run IDs;
Scheduler jobs and execution attempts;
Nodes and accelerators;
Processes, devices and ranks;
Containers and runtimes;
Steps, phases and checkpoints.
This context must travel with the telemetry or be reconstructed. Otherwise an NVLink spike is just a device event, a long collective a runtime event, a slow step an application event.
Tied to the same run, rank and interval, they become evidence of one condition.
Distributed tracing does this for microservices, linking many services into one request path. Training needs the equivalent, but its critical path runs through steps, ranks, collectives, data delivery and synchronization barriers, not HTTP calls.
Standards like OpenTelemetry can transport and correlate the data, but a transport format does not supply training semantics. The industry still needs shared conventions for runs, ranks, devices, collectives, phases and model progress.
From GPU Utilization to Training Goodput
HPCwire has explored why GPU utilization is the wrong north star for AI inference . The same holds for training, where the outcome is valid model progress rather than served requests.
GPU utilization alone does not establish how much of the allocation contributed to useful training.
A better measure is training goodput: the share of allocated accelerator time spent on valid forward passes, backward passes and optimizer steps at the expected rate.
No single metric captures it, but several make it visible:
Samples or tokens processed per allocated GPU-hour;
Step-time distributions and changes from a comparable baseline;
Time spent computing, communicating, waiting for data or checkpointing;
Arrival skew and execution differences among ranks;
Work discarded because of failures, restarts or invalid results;
Loss, gradient and checkpoint progression correlated with resource consumption.
They don’t replace hardware telemetry; they give it operational meaning.
The important question changes from “Were the GPUs busy?” to “What progress did the training run achieve with the GPU time it consumed?”
Correlation Is Necessary, But Not Sufficient
(AntonKhrupinArt/Shutterstock)
Placing signals on one timeline helps, but correlation alone does not prove causation.
A storage-latency spike during a slow step may be the cause, a side effect or someone else’s workload. A hardware error may explain a straggler, or be a corrected event with no effect on the job.
Diagnosis needs additional context: which signal changed first, how the affected rank compares with its peers, which phase the job was in, and what topology, configuration and comparable past runs suggest.
Rules, statistical baselines, causal graphs or ML models can do this analysis. AI assistants can help navigate the evidence but cannot compensate for missing identity and context.
The output should also remain explainable. Instead of declaring that “the network is slow,” a diagnostic system should be able to trace the chain from the straggler example above: one late rank, its peers waiting, the fabric healthy throughout.
That evidence chain is more useful than an anomaly score because engineers can verify it and choose the appropriate action.
Observability Must Not Become the Failure
Collecting deeper training information introduces another challenge: the observer is often closer to the workload than it is in conventional infrastructure monitoring.
CUDA is asynchronous, so host API time is not device time. As NVIDIA describes , an NCCL collective spans application calls, runtime queues, kernel launches and GPU execution; measuring one part gives a precise-looking but misleading result.
Instrumentation can also compete for buffers, hardware counters and profiler interfaces, add overhead, lose records or behave differently across CUDA, NCCL and framework versions.
That argues for a progressive collection model rather than enabling every possible profiler across an entire fleet.
A broad, low-overhead infrastructure baseline can remain active continuously. Runtime-level signals can add information about CUDA calls, collective state and rank behavior. Detailed device tracing can be enabled selectively for jobs that require it. Hardware-counter profiling can remain an explicit diagnostic operation rather than an unattended default.
The collection path must be observable too. Missing kernel records can mean no kernels ran, or that instrumentation failed; a trustworthy system must tell “no activity” from “no coverage.”
The safest design collects not the most data but enough independent evidence to diagnose the workload without unacceptable risk to the run.
A New Operational Discipline
The missing layer, then, is not GPU monitoring, experiment tracking or profiling alone, but the system that connects their evidence around what organizations care about: the training run.
Building it is a new discipline, spanning SRE, HPC performance engineering, distributed systems and machine learning; none has the whole answer alone.
When a thousand GPUs spend an hour waiting for one delayed rank, the cluster has not experienced a thousand independent utilization problems. It has experienced one distributed training problem expressed across a thousand devices.
The next generation of observability must be designed to see the difference.
About the author: Evgeny Potapov is a software engineer and technology founder with 25 years of experience in performance engineering, SRE, DevOps and distributed systems. He is a co-founder of RidgeScope , which develops observability and diagnostic technology for large-scale AI training.
